newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan visit to S.Africa seeks to ease China blow.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan visit to S.Africa seeks to ease China blow.

text.p: Taiwan's foreign minister was due to begin a damage-control mission to deserting ally South Africa on Monday as newspapers reported signs Taipei was intensifying efforts to prevent further diplomatic losses to rival China.

Minister John Chang was scheduled to depart for South Africa late on Monday to campaign for highest possible bilateral links following Pretoria's announcement on November 27 that it would sever ties with Taipei and recognise Beijing in 1997.
Analysts said the trip could backfire if Chang carried what one called the "romantic hope" that Pretoria might change its mind.

Signalling Taipei's fear that the South African decision would shake the loyalty of its handful of other allies, Vice President Lien Chan has decided to visit Nicaragua and other diplomatic partners in central America in January, newspapers said.
A foreign ministry official said he could not confirm the reports.

Chang has warned that China, having successfully courted South Africa, would now target the rest of Taipei's 29 allies -- mostly impoverished African and central American states as well as the Vatican -- to complete Taiwan's diplomatic isolation.
Eager to counter the Pretoria loss, the foreign ministry said the Micronesian island of Palau would send a team to Taiwan on December 12 to "discuss affairs involving upgrading ties".
"The visit by the delegation will improve the cooperative relations between the two sides," a ministry official quoted spokesman Peter Cheng as saying.
Cheng, however, declined to say whether Taipei and Palau would establish formal ties.
Palau has no diplomatic relations with Taiwan or China but has warm business ties with Taiwan's ruling Nationalist Party, which pledged US$8 million in 1995 to build a resort on Palau.

The Nationalists fled into exile on Taiwan after losing a civil war to the communists in 1949. Since then Beijing has regarded Taiwan as a renegade province not entitled to foreign ties and vows to retake the island, by force if necessary.

Analysts said South Africa's planned diplomatic switch, though not final until the end of 1997, was a fait accompli and Chang would be wasting Taiwan's money if he tried to persuade South African President Nelson Mandela to reverse the move.

"If he goes with the romantic hope that Mandela will change his mind, then he's going to (have to) put more resources into that hope," said Tim Ting, a politics professor at the National Taiwan University.
"It's like your girlfriend saying she's leaving you in a year and you tell her, 'I'll give you 12 roses every day until you come back'. It's impossible," Ting said.
In the past Taiwan has granted large amounts of economic aid to South Africa in the hopes of solidifying ties.
Beijing intensified its containment policy after Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui made a private U.S. visit in 1995, a move blasted by China as proof of Lee's pro-independence stand.

China mounted intimidating war games in waters near Taiwan in the months before the island's March presidential election, which Lee won in a landslide, and has stepped up pressure on Taiwan's diplomatic allies to switch ties to Beijing.
